title_en: Everything in Markets Is Now Moving Incredibly Fast
title_zh: Sherwood News 市场主管 Luke Kawa：市场里的一切现在都动得极快
subtitle_zh: Luke Kawa 用「速度」定义 2026 年的市场：AI 硬件冲劲、债市上行与分化交易。
description: Everything in Markets Is Now Moving Incredibly Fast

turns.en: Tracy, this, it dawned on me the other day, the market's kind of crazy right now. No, no, it's like seriously, it's like we're sort of used to all this stuff and everything and that. And then one day, one moment, I realized, oh, markets are really crazy these days.

turns.en: I would say weird. I find them very weird at the moment with like the biggest tension being what's happening in the bond market and the stock market. By the way, I have a huge caveat for this episode, which is we're recording this on September 29th. I've been away for the past week on vacation. I probably should have put up my like normal going on vacation warning. So something is about to blow up. Turns out it was the bond market.
turns.zh: 我会说是「怪异」。我觉得眼下市场非常怪，最大的张力就在于债市和股市正在发生的事。顺便说一句，这期节目我有个很大的前提要说明，就是我们是在 9 月 29 日录的。过去一周我休假去了。我本该像平常那样发个「我要去休假了」的预警。所以总有什么东西要爆。结果爆的是债市。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.zh: 其实你这么说挺有意思的，因为我现在看市场的方式是：发生了太多事，但从某种具体意义上说又什么都没发生。就好比，好吧，我们正处在一场跟 Iran 的战争当中。这么多事儿，我们却只是「哦，就一条头条新闻而已」。Trump 说谈判进展顺利，然后大家就翻篇了。某家 AI 公司又搞出了什么疯狂的模型跃迁之类的，是重大新闻，但如今这种节奏太规律了，以至于连这个都几乎变成了噪音。当然债市的波动，我猜，那大概是唯一一件真正让人觉得新鲜的事，也许就在最近这几周。但即便在那里，很多那种焦虑其实已经存在很久了。所以就是，什么都有太多了，没有哪一件事能单独…… 你知道吗，我就在想，比如昨天，9 月 28 日，官宣 David Zervos 要从 Jeffries 跳槽到——

turns.en: It feels like stock markets are sort of overwhelmed and or inured to everything happening except trying to make money. No. Like that is the one impulse that remains. That never gets old.
turns.zh: 感觉股市对正在发生的一切要么是被淹没了、要么是麻木了，唯独对「赚钱」这件事例外。不，赚钱是唯一还留存的那股冲动。这事儿永远不会腻。

turns.en: No. And that's arguably the point of the whole thing. Anyway. We need like a sort of big rambling state of the markets episode. And we really do have the perfect guest, someone who used to be our colleague here at Bloomberg. We are, of course, speaking to Luke Kawa, head of markets at Sherwood News. Luke, thank you for coming back on Odd Lots.
turns.zh: 对，而且这可以说正是整件事的意义所在。总之，我们需要那种大而散、纵论市场现状的一期节目。而我们真的请到了完美的嘉宾，一位曾经是我们 Bloomberg 同事的人。我们对话的当然是 Sherwood News 的市场主管 Luke Kawa。Luke，谢谢你再次来到 Odd Lots。

turns.en: Great to be here. Thanks for having me, Al.
turns.zh: 很高兴来到这里。谢谢你们邀请我。

turns.en: Let me start on something niche, actually, because there's so much going on. Suddenly, lately, markets are having a great year. S & P up over 12% or about that as the time I'm talking. I see a lot of talk about breadth. This is, everyone's talking about market breadth these days.
turns.zh: 让我先从一个小众的话题说起，因为发生的事情太多了。突然间，最近市场这一年过得很不错。S&P 上涨了超过 12%，或者差不多这个数，就在我说话的这会儿。我看到很多关于「市场广度」（breadth）的讨论。这就是——最近人人都在聊市场广度。

turns.en: What's that all about? Yeah, I think why they're talking about breadth is because it's absolutely god-awful. There's been a lot of different stats to show it. You can say the average stat is XYZ, below its high. Well, the S & P 500 is, you know, as of writing about, you know, 1.5% off of its high. The one I came up with that bothered a lot of people the other day was, coming into this week, the S & P 500 was 0.5% off record high. Mm-hmm. just 51.2% of stocks were above their 200 day. The last time we had that proximity to a high with that few stocks above the 200 day was literally the day after the dot-com bubble peak. So that gets a lot of people mad, but then you have to point out, okay, wait, breadth was also that bad in 1998. The market ripped for another two years after that. So it really is a case of, and I think to unify a lot of what you were talking about in the intro, Is the market inert to higher rates? No, a lot of the market isn't. The S & P 500 equal weight certainly isn't. The Russell 2000 certainly isn't. However, basically, to me, there seems to be just this big bet that the AI impulse will continue to eat and swallow the world until who knows what puts a stop to it, whether that's kind of credit conditions, the capacity to lend, whether that's regulation. But right now, the pricing to me just looks like more and more betting on a singular factor to be able to drive growth. Think about it. When's the last time that there seemed to be more confidence in European industrials than the US consumer during a period of strong growth? I cannot ever remember that happening outside of maybe like Euro boom, what was it, 2017 for a couple months.
turns.zh: 这到底是怎么回事？对，我觉得大家之所以在聊广度，是因为它简直糟透了。有很多不同的数据都能说明这一点。你可以说某个平均指标是 XYZ，低于它的高点。可 S&P 500，你知道，截至我写稿时大约离它的高点也就 1.5%。我前几天想出来的那个、惹恼了很多人的数据是：进入本周时，S&P 500 离历史高点只差 0.5%。嗯。可只有 51.2% 的成分股在它们的 200 日均线上方。上一次我们离高点这么近、却在 200 日均线上方的股票这么少，恰恰就是互联网泡沫见顶后的第二天。所以这让很多人很恼火，但你又必须指出，好吧，等等，1998 年的广度也一样糟。之后市场又猛涨了两年。所以这真的是一个……我觉得，把你开场讲的那些串起来看，问题就是：市场对更高的利率麻木了吗？不，市场的很大一部分并不麻木。S&P 500 等权指数肯定不麻木。Russell 2000 肯定也不麻木。但基本上，在我看来，就是有这样一个大的押注：AI 的这股冲劲会继续吞噬、席卷整个世界，直到不知道什么东西让它停下来——不管是信贷状况、放贷能力，还是监管。但眼下，这种定价在我看来就是越来越多地押注于单一因素能够驱动增长。想想看，上一次在强劲增长时期，大家对 European 工业股的信心似乎超过对 US 消费者的信心，是什么时候？除了大概 2017 年那几个月 Euro 景气期之外，我完全想不起有过这种情况。

turns.en: I mean, it is true that in higher rates, so rates are a blunt tool for the Fed, right? And they're going to hurt something like a home builder a lot more than an AI company that is issuing like mega deals into the bond market, I would imagine. Is it the case that, you know, maybe the bet on AI makes sense in that environment? Maybe the AI companies are the ones that are less rate sensitive than a lot of other businesses out there.
turns.zh: 我是说，在利率更高的环境里确实如此，利率对 Fed 来说是个很钝的工具，对吧？我想，它对一个房建商的伤害，会远大于对一家正在债市上发行巨额融资的 AI 公司的伤害。那么，会不会是这样：在那种环境下押注 AI 是说得通的？也许 AI 公司正是那些相比外面很多其他企业、对利率没那么敏感的。

turns.en: I think right now that's like a perfect encapsulation of conventional wisdom. To me, it's also very interesting that as we've had this latest explosion higher in yields and we've talked about like, oh, it's the AI impulse this, that. It's also come at a time where hyperscaler credit spreads, none of them are at their wides of the year at the long end. It comes after a September of, you can tell me how much USIG and USIG issuance there was by hyperscalers. I believe that's a zero for September. So it's, yeah, so very, very interesting.
turns.zh: 我觉得眼下这正好是传统智慧（conventional wisdom）的完美概括。对我来说，同样很有意思的是，就在收益率最新这一轮爆发式上行、我们说什么「哦，是 AI 冲劲这那那」的时候，超大规模云计算厂商（hyperscaler）的信用利差，在长端没有一个处在年内最宽的水平。而这是在这样一个 9 月之后——你来告诉我 hyperscaler 在 USIG（美国投资级）上发了多少债吧。我记得 9 月是零。所以，是啊，非常非常有意思。

turns.en: They cut back a lot because they got a little bit spooked with the CapEx response from the market.
turns.zh: 他们大幅削减了发行，因为市场对 CapEx 的反应把他们吓着了一点。

turns.en: So that to me is something that like, hey, a lot of this in the bond market, both a response to stronger growth and the potential for issuance, a lot of this is like the classic Mark Dow belated overreaction to something we've been thinking and talking about for a long while. And then I think the, the question is how long can the cyclicals that are doing well, you know, operationally, at least how long can you, they be plumbing 52 week lows, a lot of these, and is it just because AI is doing so well? And I think that's the kind of important part to be making the important point to be making that so much of this market has been dispersion. Helene Meisler calls it the either or market. I've called it, you know, the Elaine George market, Jerry's friends, only one can do well at the right time. But that's been a really, really defining trademark of 2026. At first it was semi-software. I think more recently it's been like this idea of inertia stocks versus the general AI beneficiaries. And that to me is a bit of an important twist. It's this idea that like It's not just one layer of AI that benefits. It's multiple layers through software, through the hardware providers that get to benefit from an impulse like Muse, like Agentic Commerce, and then others that get hit. So that to me is at least a bit of a nuance in how the market treats AI and the impulse. But for me, it's just really a sign of the mechanics that have continued to dominate and just continuing to play out.
turns.zh: 所以那对我来说意味着，嘿，债市里的很多东西，既有对更强增长的回应、也有对潜在发行的回应，很多都像是经典的 Mark Dow 式的、对我们思考并谈论了很久的东西的迟到过度反应。然后我觉得，问题是那些经营层面表现不错的周期股，还能探 52 周新低探多久——这里面很多都在创新低——难道仅仅是因为 AI 表现太好了吗？我觉得这才是要点所在，要讲的重要观点是：这个市场太多的部分一直是「分化」（dispersion）。Helene Meisler 管它叫「非此即彼市场」（either/or market）。我则叫它，你知道，「Elaine、George 市场」——Jerry 的朋友们，同一时间只有一个能过得好。但这一直是 2026 年一个非常非常有定义性的标志。一开始是半导体 vs 软件。我觉得最近则是这种「惯性股 vs 广义 AI 受益者」的概念。而这在我看来是一个挺重要的转折。就是说，受益的不只是 AI 的某一层，而是多层——通过软件、通过那些硬件供应商，它们能从像 Muse、像 Agentic Commerce 这样的冲劲中获益，然后另一些则被打击。所以这在我看来至少是市场如何对待 AI 及这股冲劲的一个细微差别。但对我来说，它真的只是一个信号，表明那些一直占据主导的机制在继续演绎下去。

turns.en: It's interesting.
turns.zh: 这很有意思。

turns.en: I looked up a chart of McDonald's and... That was doing really well up until, and then it peaked on March 3rd and then it's been straight down. So it's like basically when the Iran war started, that was.
turns.zh: 我查了一下 McDonald's 的走势图，它一直表现很好，直到…… 然后在 3 月 3 日见顶，之后就一路下跌。所以基本上就是 Iran 战争开始那会儿，那就是拐点。

turns.en: Wait, was that when the CEO ate- Oh.
turns.zh: 等等，那是不是 CEO 吃了——那个…… 哦。

turns.en: Reluctantly ate part of the cheeseburger? I forgot about that. But it's just like any consumer name you can think of right now. The stock is awful. Nike is the classic example.
turns.zh: 勉为其难地咬了一口那个芝士汉堡？我都忘了这茬了。但就是你现在能想到的任何消费类股票，走势都很糟。Nike 就是经典例子。

turns.en: That's crazy.
turns.zh: 太疯狂了。

turns.en: That was $ 180 stock in 2021. It's 35 now. I mean, there's just like I mean, granted, it had a huge run up in 2021, too. But like any like just sort of like regular business that is they're just doing terrible.
turns.zh: 2021 年它可是 180 美元的股票。现在只有 35 了。我是说，当然，它 2021 年也有过一波 huge 的上涨。但就是任何那种普普通通的生意，现在都做得很糟糕。

turns.en: It's it's crazy. Like and when you look at Nike, one of the things that stands out and I think you could apply this more recently to a Walmart, possibly to a Costco. And I'll tie this back to software, oddly enough. But these were relatively expensive stocks that didn't have exceptional top line growth. in a world where nominal growth has been accelerating. That's been what the bond market move is about. That's what stock market resilience is about. Why do you want to own those stocks? Why do you want to own the stocks that aren't growing that fast, that are expensive, when everything else is growing very fast? So I think for what happened for a while is that a lot of these consumer names, Walmart and Costco in particular, they were stand-ins for the software stocks that were bound to be disrupted by AI. Because if you think about it, if you're going to spend a certain amount at Walmart every month. That looks to me like an ARR kind of revenue profile that you've got there. Costco is literally a subscription kind of membership in a lot of ways. So I think that was a stand-in for disruption fears. And as software has come back, you've seen kind of multiples there deflate. So I think it is, we got to find someone to punish. Maybe it's just because everyone's very invested, but when AI is doing well, you got to find someone to punish.
turns.zh: 太疯狂了。你看 Nike，有一点很突出，而且我觉得这一点最近也能套用到 Walmart 身上，可能还有 Costco。说来奇怪，我会把它跟软件联系起来。这些都是估值相对偏贵、营收（top line）增长又不算出色的股票，而这个世界里名义增长一直在加速。债市那波行情讲的就是这个。股市的韧性讲的也是这个。你为什么想持有那些股票？在别的 everything 都增长得非常快的时候，你为什么想持有那些增长没那么快、又贵的股票？所以我觉得有一段时间发生的情况是，很多这类消费股，尤其是 Walmart 和 Costco，它们成了那些注定会被 AI 颠覆的软件股的替身。因为你想，如果你每个月都要在 Walmart 花掉一定的钱，那在我看来，你手上就是一份类似 ARR（年度经常性收入）的营收结构。Costco 在很多方面根本就是一种订阅式会员。所以我觉得那就是「颠覆恐惧」的替身。而随着软件股回升，你就会看到那边的估值倍数被压下去。所以我觉得，就是这么回事：我们得找个对象来惩罚。也许只是因为大家都押得很重，但当 AI 表现好的时候，你就得找个对象来惩罚。

turns.en: What about just in terms of pure earnings expectations, what we're seeing here? Because this is the other thing that in theory should be happening, which is you hear about productivity gains from AI. You should be seeing people get excited about the possibility of cutting labor costs, I don't know, coming up with new products with AI or whatever. And in theory, you should be seeing that go into the earnings estimates for future years. Are we seeing any of that?
turns.zh: 那单纯从业绩预期（earnings expectations）的角度看，我们这里看到的又是什么？因为这是另一件理论上应该正在发生的事：你听到 AI 带来的生产率提升。你应该看到人们为削减劳动力成本的可能性而兴奋，或者，我不知道，用 AI 搞出新产品之类的。理论上，你应该看到这些进入未来几年的盈利预估里。我们看到任何这样的迹象了吗？

turns.en: I would say in theory and in practice, what we continue to see more of is the AI hardware impulse as just the straight fuel for earnings. Goldman had a good note released a couple of days ago where they said about half of earnings growth this year is expected to be just driven by hyperscaler CapEx. So pretty, pretty big impulse. We're talking about how strong growth has been, earnings growth has been this year. And you can just link it and distill it just down to that one factor. And then also, if you look at, okay, they also ran in a separate note. what do we think explains multiples across Russell 1000 stocks? And the answer they came up with was more so than usual, it's three years forward sales estimates. Right now, the one year forward sales estimates and those revisions have almost no explanatory power. So sales growth right now and for the near future, it's priced in. We all know it. We see the backlogs, all this, all that. The real bet on what you're willing to pay for is the kind of three years out thing. And when I did a scan of stocks that were just both expensive and had so markets willing to reward them and fairly high sales estimates. Your bloom energies, a lot of the optic stocks, those are the ones that pop out there. So that's been kind of the way to earn a higher valuation right now. In this market, it's betting on the continuation of the hardware trade.
turns.zh: 我会说，无论在理论上还是实践中，我们持续看到更多的，是 AI 硬件这股冲劲直接充当盈利的燃料。Goldman 前几天发了一份很好的报告，他们说今年盈利增长里预计大约有一半就是由 hyperscaler 的 CapEx 驱动的。所以是相当、相当大的冲劲。我们在讲今年增长、盈利增长有多强，而你可以直接把它归结、提炼到那一个因素上。然后还有，如果你看，好吧，他们在另一份报告里还研究了：我们认为是什么在解释 Russell 1000 各只股票的估值倍数？他们得出的答案是，比往常更甚——是三年期的前瞻营收预估。眼下，一年期前瞻营收预估及其修正几乎没有解释力。所以当下以及近未来的营收增长，已经被 price in 了。我们都知道，我们看得到那些订单积压（backlog），这一切那些。你愿意为之付费的真正押注，是那种三年之外的东西。当我扫描了那些既贵、市场又愿意奖励它们、且营收预估相当高的股票时，你的 Bloom Energy、很多光模块（optic）股，就是跳出来的那些。所以这就是眼下赢得更高估值的方式。在这个市场里，就是押注硬件交易的延续。

turns.en: Yeah, this is something interesting. Both Tracy and I love the hair charts, the Medusa charts of all sorts, where you see historical expectations of trajectory. And one of the ones you're starting to see more is just the CapEx one. And so you look at what sell side had estimated hyperscaler CapEx would be in 2023 and over the next three years. And then that keeps getting revised higher. And it seems like it's continuous. And so I'm curious, there is some number exists, right? So maybe, I don't know what it is. They'll say like, okay, they're expected to spend 1.2 trillion over X period of time. And that's up. But how much of the trade is essentially a trade that then the estimates will keep getting revised higher for spending.
turns.zh: 对，这有个有意思的点。Tracy 和我都喜欢那种「头发图」、各种「Medusa 图」，就是你能看到历史预期的轨迹那种。而你开始越来越多看到的一张，就是 CapEx 那张。你看卖方在 2023 年时预估 hyperscaler 的 CapEx 在未来三年会是多少，然后那个数字不断被上修。看起来是持续不断的。所以我很好奇，确实存在某个具体数字，对吧？也许，我不知道是多少，他们会说，好吧，预计在 X 段时间内花 1.2 万亿。而且还在往上。但这笔交易里，有多少本质上是在押「支出预估还会不断被上修」这件事？

turns.en: I got to think a solid chunk right now. And there's at some point, I think there has to be this handoff from that to a kind of more broader set. And when NVIDIA, and it was either a quarter ago or one before that, they actually kind of rejiggered how they're organizing... their earnings to account for the fact that we expect sovereign AI and robotics and physical AI on-prem stuff. We expect that to be contributing more and more to our sales going forward. It's going to be real small now to start, but we expect that to be a bigger driver than hyperscalers and potentially neoclouds, but they're doing all they can to support that. going forward. So I think right now that is a huge, huge chunk of the trade, the bulk of the trade. But the promise of AI is that it has to be more applicable than that, right? To your point, it has to have the productivity booms. It has to have the labor saving. If it doesn't, then what are we here for is kind of, I think, the question at some point.
turns.zh: 我觉得现在这是相当大的一块。而且在某个时点，我认为必须有一个从这块向更广的一组东西的「交接」。当 NVIDIA——那要么是一个季度前、要么再往前一个季度——他们其实重新调整了组织业绩的方式，来反映这样一个事实：我们预期 sovereign AI、机器人以及本地部署（on-prem）的物理 AI，将对我们未来的销售贡献越来越多。起步时会非常小，但我们预期它会成为比 hyperscaler、乃至潜在的 neocloud 更大的驱动力，而且他们正竭尽全力去支撑它。所以我觉得眼下这是这笔交易里巨大、巨大的一块，是交易的主体。但 AI 的承诺在于，它必须比这更广泛地适用，对吧？就像你说的，它得带来生产率的爆发，得带来劳动力的节省。如果没有，那么「我们到底为了什么」，我觉得，在某个时点就会成为那个问题。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Did you see the chart? I think it was in Adam Tooze's newsletter this morning saying that The CapEx expenditure on AI is now like the biggest.
turns.zh: 你看到那张图了吗？我记得是今早 Adam Tooze 的 newsletter 里说的，说 AI 上的 CapEx 支出现在已经是最大的——

turns.en: Infrastructure boom of all time.
turns.zh: 有史以来最大的基建热潮。

turns.en: Oh, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，对，对。

turns.en: There have been two great papers.
turns.zh: 有两篇很好的论文。

turns.en: I saw the economist Hannah Lustig, I'm not sure if I'm pronouncing his name right, who's saying that to justify all the spending that they estimate, like a handful of companies will have to get revenue that's like 9% of GDP in order to justify it, which is just like unbelievable.
turns.zh: 我看到那位经济学家 Hannah Lustig——我不确定我名字发音对不对——他说，要证成他们估算的所有这些支出，少数几家公司将必须拿到相当于 GDP 大约 9% 的营收，才能说得过去，这简直难以置信。

turns.en: It's ambitious. Ambitious.
turns.zh: 这很有野心。相当有野心。

turns.en: I'll put it that way. So I promised myself I wasn't going to talk exclusively fixed income in this conversation, but we can't have Fluke on without talking more about fixed income. Bond yields rising. So these are the headlines that I saw when I was on vacation last week. The 10-year going to above 5%, 30-year rising as well. What's your story for, I guess I should divide it up, global bond yields rising and then U.S. Treasury yields rising specifically?
turns.zh: 我就这么说吧。我之前跟自己保证，这场对话不会只聊固定收益，但请 Luke 上节目又不聊更多固收是说不过去的。债券收益率在上行。这些是我上周休假时看到的头条：10 年期升破 5%，30 年期也在上行。你的解释是什么——我想我应该分开来讲：全球债券收益率上行，以及具体到 U.S. Treasury 收益率上行？

turns.en: Predominantly, I think it's the same story for both or the same. Like if you had to do a principal component analysis or something, I think what would stick out across the board is it's the global growth impulse. It's activity. It's both in the U.S. and globally. I think we see the industrial side of every economy is doing incredibly well and expected to do so. And I think something you wrote a while ago kind of fits into this about that which can be repurposed for AI will be with reference to Ford. I believe that it seems as though the impulse is just getting more widely shared. You have an impulse this big, it's bound to lift a lot of boats. And I would say that's kind of what's happening throughout the global economy. That is far and away, I would say, the one thing to think of if you just had an elevator pitch with someone, why are bond yields high? Because growth is really strong, that's putting inflation up, and central banks are expected to respond to that.
turns.zh: 主要地，我觉得两者是同一个故事，或者说是一样的。就像如果你得做个主成分分析（principal component analysis）之类的，我认为全面凸显出来的，就是全球增长的冲劲，是经济活动，在美国和全球都是如此。我觉得我们看到每个经济体的工业端都表现得极其出色，而且预期会继续这样。我觉得你不久前写的一句话正好契合这一点：凡是能被改造用于 AI 的东西都会被改造——我记得是拿 Ford 来说的。看起来这股冲劲正变得越来越被广泛分享。你有这么大的冲劲，它必然会托起很多条船。我会说这大致就是整个全球经济正在发生的事。如果你只能跟某人来个「电梯陈述」，那这绝对是首要的一点：为什么债券收益率这么高？因为增长非常强劲，这在推高通胀，而央行被预期会对此作出回应。

turns.en: Wait, but we haven't had a huge move in break-evens in the US, for instance.
turns.zh: 等等，但比如在美国，我们的盈亏平衡通胀率（break-evens）并没有大幅变动。

turns.en: Yeah, but I think that somewhat speaks to the idea that central banks are going to be quote-unquote credible in keeping a lid on inflation over time. You can believe that or not, because if you've been a hold to maturity buyer of five-year US treasuries from at any point in 2011 to 2021, outside of like a little before the shale bust, if you got in there, you have negative real returns for the entire period.
turns.zh: 对，但我觉得这在某种程度上说明了一个观点：央行将会是——打个引号——「可信的」，能长期把通胀压住。你信不信随你，因为如果你在 2011 到 2021 年间任意一个时点买入五年期 US Treasury 并持有到期，除了页岩油崩盘前那一小段之外，只要你在那个区间进场，整个期间的实际回报都是负的。

turns.en: I'm actually very curious. I find this, the stability of breakevens to be very surprising because usually what people say is like, well, yeah, naturally people think the Fed is going to take its dual mandate seriously. And okay, we're going to, they're going to have to raise rates to roughly, I think it's, and Therefore, inflation will be a little over 2%. Are you surprised that after years and years of the Fed missing its inflation target, there hasn't been more like, no, we do not think, we do not have the confidence that the Fed will be able to maintain stable inflation in the years ahead? Or why isn't it manifesting on that chart? Oh.
turns.zh: 我其实非常好奇。我觉得盈亏平衡通胀率这么稳定，非常令人意外。因为通常大家的说法是，好吧，是啊，人们自然会认为 Fed 会认真对待它的双重使命（dual mandate）。行，他们将被迫把利率加到大致——我想是多少来着——因此通胀会比 2% 略高一点。你会不会觉得意外：在 Fed 连续这么多年都没达到通胀目标之后，市场却没有更多那种「不，我们不认为、我们没有信心 Fed 能在未来几年维持稳定的通胀」的情绪？或者说，为什么它没有体现在那张图上？哦。

turns.en: I would say in a word, yes. I'm genuinely surprised by that.
turns.zh: 我会用一个字回答：是。我对此是真的感到意外。

turns.en: Yeah, I find this really surprising.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得这真的很令人意外。

turns.en: I think it is an odd dynamic. The best explanation I have for it is just thinking back to when I'd be in meetings and we're discussing asset allocation, especially during 2022 at UBS and 2023, high inflation environment. Basically, bonds become the residual at a certain point. Like You buy bonds when you're worried about growth and you don't think there's going to be that much inflation. If you think growth is fine and it's inflationary, well, you know, it's cash or short term and a lot of stocks or stocks, commodities, a little bit of cash. So it's just like bonds are kind of the thing you make the final decision on. So I would say the fact that a lot of this is driven by real yields might come back to a thing of like, How do we get bonds to be more attractive relative to stocks? And a lot of people will do your earnings yield less the plain vanilla yield on bonds. You should probably be doing it versus the real yield. Stock earnings are more of a real stream of assets. So I think in order to get bonds to be a more competitive asset with stocks, you do need to see reals rising and that a lot of the move is effectively saying like, hey, I can't justify buying a 2% even real return, 3% real return when. This is what I think is on offer in AI. So I think having it come through reels is part of that story and part of why part of the decision-making process in terms of how a cross asset investor would be looking at bonds.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是一种奇怪的动态。我能给出的最好解释，就是回想我以前开会讨论资产配置的时候，尤其是在 UBS 的 2022 年和 2023 年那种高通胀环境。基本上，债券到某个点就成了「剩下的那一项」（residual）。就是说，当你担心增长、又觉得不会有那么多通胀时，你才买债券。如果你觉得增长没问题、而且是通胀性的，那么，你懂的，就是现金或短端，加大量股票，或者股票、大宗商品、一点点现金。所以债券有点像你最后才做决定的那个东西。因此我会说，这波行情很大程度上由实际收益率（real yields）驱动，这个事实可能又回到一个问题：我们怎么才能让债券相对于股票更有吸引力？很多人会用你的盈利收益率减去债券那个最普通的收益率。但你大概应该拿它去对比实际收益率。股票盈利更像是一种实际的资产流。所以我觉得，要让债券成为一个相对股票更有竞争力的资产，你确实需要看到实际收益率上行；而这波行情里很大一部分其实是在说，嘿，当我认为 AI 提供的回报是这样的，我就没法为一个 2%、哪怕 3% 的实际回报买单。所以我觉得它通过实际收益率体现出来，是这个故事的一部分，也是跨资产投资者如何看待债券这个决策过程的一部分。

turns.en: Or you go the financial repression route and just make everyone hold bonds, right? That's like, that's an actual possibility.
turns.zh: 或者你走金融抑制（financial repression）这条路，直接让所有人都持有债券，对吧？这算是——这是一种真实存在的可能性。

turns.en: Or we need to have a big national campaign to to get people to stop spending money and to put their money into AI bonds a la war bonds, right?
turns.zh: 或者我们需要搞一场全国性的运动，让人们别再花钱，把钱投进「AI 债券」，就像当年的战争债券（war bonds）那样，对吧？

turns.en: I mean, yeah, with people already putting some weight on PDoom with not liking the noise from data centers and their environment, I think what America needs right now is to be told to spend less so that the AI boom can more fully run its course. I'm not running as a third party candidate and I'm also probably not allowed, but that would be definitely my platform.
turns.zh: 我是说，是啊，既然人们已经开始给 PDoom 赋予一些权重、又不喜欢数据中心及其环境带来的噪音，我觉得美国现在需要的，就是被告知要少花钱，好让 AI 繁荣能更充分地走完它的过程。我不是要作为第三党候选人参选，而且我大概也不被允许，但那绝对会是我的竞选纲领。

turns.en: I would classify that under financial repression, but I'm sure you see it differently.
turns.zh: 我会把它归到金融抑制那一类，不过我相信你的看法不一样。

turns.en: It is a form of financial repression. Yeah, yeah, totally. Just make it patriotic. This is actually a worrisome dynamic to me in thinking about the economy, which is people perceive that AI supremacy is going to be crucial for national security, right? I believe this is a widely held view in Washington, etc., If we actually then took that idea seriously, we would be saying, yeah, we want to depress the non-AI parts of the economy to free up real resources for the build-out, et cetera. Clearly, no one can say this or articulate this or say, we're going to tax consumption of this. We're going to tax consumption of boats, anything that could be stripped for its parts to be put into a data center, et cetera. But- if it is a matter of like existential national security, that would be the way we would be doing policy.
turns.zh: 它就是一种金融抑制。对，对，完全是。把它包装成爱国就行了。这其实是我在思考经济时觉得令人担忧的一个动态：人们认为 AI 霸权将对国家安全至关重要，对吧？我相信这在 Washington 等地是被广泛持有的观点。如果我们真的把这个想法当回事，我们就会说，是的，我们想压制经济中非 AI 的部分，好为这场建设腾出实际资源，等等。显然，没人能把这话说出口、或者清楚表述出来，说我们要对这种消费征税，我们要对游艇消费征税，对任何能被拆掉零件塞进数据中心的东西征税，等等。但如果这真是一件关乎存亡的国家安全问题，那就会是我们制定政策的方式。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Almost certainly. And then you have to go like with, man, if I'm being told I can't still can't buy a house because of the, that's, that's going to bother the hell out of me. So I think there is, and it's not like, and it's.
turns.zh: 几乎可以肯定。然后你就得面对这种情况：老天，如果告诉我，因为这，我还是买不起房，那会把我烦死。所以我觉得确实存在这种张力，而且它又不像……而且它……

turns.en: Not like the nuclear, the nuclear race where once a country has achieved a bomb, it is then in the club of nuclear powers. There's like, it's never ending because it's like, there's no like reason to presume. It's like, Oh, we got the capabilities here.
turns.zh: 不像核竞赛——核竞赛里一旦一个国家造出了原子弹，它就进入了核俱乐部。而这个（AI 竞赛）像是永无止境的，因为没有一个理由可以假定「哦，我们已经具备了这个能力」就到此为止。

turns.en: And when I, hear that, what I immediately think of is, damn, we don't know how easy we had it, speaking as a policymaker, back in the post-GFC era. There were no, like, did trade-offs exist?
turns.zh: 当我听到这个，我立刻想到的是：该死，我们根本不知道自己当年过得有多轻松——站在政策制定者的角度说，在全球金融危机（GFC）之后的那段时期。（那时）根本不存在什么取舍，对吧？取舍存在吗？

turns.en: Did trade-offs do.
turns.zh: 取舍存在过吗。

turns.en: Not exist for an entire cycle? We still probably didn't do it optimally, but pretty darn close. And now I grew up hearing about how central banks- just by virtue of saying inflation was going to be 2%, that was one of the important factors that would help it be 2% over time. I think now we're learning that that's junk that, completely junk that. You got to prove it over time or else you will be in a situation we are right now where people really apparently don't like to hold bonds.
turns.zh: 整整一个周期里都不存在？我们那时可能也没做到最优，但已经相当接近了。而现在——我从小听到的说法是，央行光是宣称通胀会是 2%，这本身就是帮助它长期维持在 2% 的重要因素之一。我觉得现在我们在学到，那完全是废话、彻底的废话。你必须随着时间证明给它看，否则你就会陷入我们现在这种局面：人们显然真的很不喜欢持有债券。

turns.en: So Joe described this as a crazy market. I described it as a weird market. Can you choose your one word for describing the market? And then you're over at Robinhood now. I'm sure you see some interesting retail investment trends and color, and maybe a little bit of flow. Like, what are you seeing at the moment?
turns.zh: Joe 把这形容成一个疯狂的市场。我形容成一个怪异的市场。你能选一个你自己的词来形容这个市场吗？还有，你现在在 Robinhood。我相信你会看到一些有意思的散户投资趋势和细节，也许还有一点资金流。你眼下看到了什么？

turns.en: Yeah. So if I had to summarize the cross asset, how I see it, like last year ago was Tina. And there is no alternative. Yes, there is no alternative. This is too fast to fade both prices and earnings, just moving too fast to fade. And speed is something that I think has completely defined 2026. If you look at the monthly change between semis and software, Those have had some of its most four violent moves in either direction this year alone. I remember when Silver was going crazy, but that was this year. Absolutely nuts moves all over the place. And to make this an AI thing, we were being told AI compresses economic time. And I think that was both because the power of the technology, the need to be able to look forward and see what has disrupted. And now because of agents who can work when we're asleep. So this idea of a compression of time and speed manifesting in the markets is really, really what sticks out to me. And in terms of the retail side, the trading I've seen, so I can describe net single stock purchases at Robinhood. So the absolute peak for that, the rolling 21 day peak happened right about in late June, let's call it. So around Micron's earnings then, that was the overall peak. There was one before that in early November 2025, which coincided roughly with a really big spec asset peak, in my view, in October 2025. That's still, in some senses, we haven't fully recovered from. So a spec? A spec asset, like a lot of things, like Palantir, Bitcoin, quantum stocks, so many of these things.
turns.zh: 好。如果要我总结跨资产的看法——我怎么看——一年前是 TINA（there is no alternative，别无选择）。而现在，「没有替代」变成了「涨得太快，无法去做空」（too fast to fade），价格和盈利都是，动得太快，你没法逆势去做。而「速度」这一点，我觉得完全定义了 2026 年。如果你看半导体和软件之间的月度变化，光今年一年，它们就出现了双向中最剧烈的一些波动。我记得 Silver 疯涨的时候，但那也是今年。到处都是绝对疯狂的走势。而且要把它归到 AI 这件事上：我们一直被告知 AI 会压缩经济时间。我觉得这既是因为技术的力量、需要能够向前看并预见到什么会被颠覆，现在也是因为那些能在我们睡觉时干活的 agent。所以这种「时间和速度被压缩」并体现在市场上的想法，真的是、真的最让我印象深刻。至于散户这边，我看到的交易——我可以讲讲 Robinhood 上的单只股票净买入。它的绝对峰值、那个滚动的 21 日峰值，大约就出现在 6 月下旬，就这么说吧。也就是 Micron 财报那前后，那是整体峰值。在那之前还有一个，在 2025 年 11 月初，大致与我眼中 2025 年 10 月一个非常大的投机资产峰值重合。那个峰值在某种意义上我们到现在都还没完全恢复过来。所以「投机资产」？很多这类东西，像 Palantir、Bitcoin、量子计算股，太多这类东西了。

turns.en: Yes, yes.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.en: And even call option volumes in total, those peaked for a while and rolled over. But that was a huge spec top that we're still kind of clawing our way back from in some senses. So there's that. And more recently, what we've seen is supposed to be traditionally a slow month, September for retail. It's really rebounded quite, quite strongly. September, last numbers I have are about 89% of the peak that we saw in June, we're back to. So it's been a really strong month for buying.
turns.zh: 甚至连总的看涨期权成交量，也在见顶一段时间后回落了。但那是个巨大的投机顶部，某种意义上我们还在艰难地往回爬。这是那一块。而更近一些，我们看到的是：对散户来说本该是传统淡季的 9 月，却反弹得相当、相当强劲。9 月，我手上最新的数据大约回到了我们在 6 月看到的峰值的 89%。所以这是一个买入非常强劲的月份。

turns.en: It's because I went on vacation and spent a lot of money.
turns.zh: 那是因为我休假去了，还花了一大笔钱。

turns.en: And a lot of it's the names you would suspect. It's your Microns, your SpaceXes, those lead it. But every day when I look at this, There's a name in the top 25. I consider myself someone who knows a lot of tickers. There is a name that I do not recognize and have to look up very often. It's fun. It's a sign of how people look for volatility. People look to get rich quick, look at options trading. Stock market is a place where we go to express our views about the long-term earnings power of corporate America. And we do it with options with four days or less to expiry. That's the story of the world we.
turns.zh: 而且很多都是你会猜到的那些名字。你的 Micron、你的 SpaceX 之类，它们在领涨。但每天我看这个榜单，前 25 里总有一个名字——我自认为是个认识很多股票代码的人——有一个我不认识、经常得去查的名字。挺有意思的。这是人们如何追逐波动性的一个标志。人们想快速致富，就去看期权交易。股市本是我们去表达对 corporate America 长期盈利能力看法的地方。而我们用的却是到期日只剩四天或更短的期权。这就是我们所处这个世界的故事——

turns.en: Live in now.
turns.zh: ——如今生活其中的世界。

turns.zh: 我看到是六月。但我很喜欢——其实我很喜欢「速度」这个框架，因为它似乎跟我引入这个话题的方式都非常相关。而那些「AI 即奇点」派的人、Kurzweil 等人谈论的一件事，就是这样一个概念：好吧，如果你用地球绕太阳一周要多久来度量时间，那是稳定的。但如果你用「多久会出现一件值得上头条的事件」来度量时间——这是一种不同的、正当地不同的度量时间的方式——这就非同寻常了。因为，这就回到了开场那句话：值得上头条的事件，其节奏之快就是非同寻常。然后你就会看到，它因此体现在你所交易的任何标的资产的价格波动速度上。

turns.en: Wait, is it headlines, though, or is there also an element of market structure in here? Because the other thing that's happened is we have a lot more pod shops that are out there that seem to be affecting the market and causing sharp swings. We have a lot more products. We have a lot more zero day call options, things like that. And this has been an ongoing trend in the market for a while where we see the mean reversals happening really, really fast now, much faster than they used to.
turns.zh: 等等，但这真的是头条新闻的原因吗，还是说这里面也有市场结构（market structure）的成分？因为另一件已经发生的事是，市面上多了很多 pod shop（多策略投资平台），它们似乎在影响市场、引发剧烈摆动。我们多了很多产品，多了很多零日到期看涨期权（zero day call options）之类的。而这已经是市场里持续了一段时间的趋势：我们看到均值回归（mean reversion）现在发生得非常、非常快，比过去快得多。

turns.en: I certainly think both the higher participation of retail, the increased AUM, if you want to call it that, in the pod shop models with tighter stops, even agentic trading, which from what I can see so far seems to be a little more Momo driven than most in terms of the rules people will put in to do this. Yeah, I think all of that and overlay the dispersion trade on top of that, I think all of that does contribute to an environment where you do get a lot more single stock volatility and a lot less at the index level. And that means even when markets are doing absolutely nothing, it's the classic duck with its feet underwater going crazy. We always have something to talk about even when the stock market is completely aimless for months.
turns.zh: 我当然认为，散户更高的参与度、pod shop 模式里增长的 AUM（如果你想这么叫的话）配以更紧的止损，甚至 agentic trading（智能体交易）——就我目前所见，从人们为此设定的规则来看，它似乎比大多数更受「追涨」（Momo，momentum）驱动——是的，我觉得所有这些，再叠加那个分化交易（dispersion trade），确实共同造就了一种环境：你会得到多得多的个股波动性，而在指数层面却少得多。这意味着，即便市场完全无所作为，也是那只经典的鸭子——水面上纹丝不动，水下的脚却在疯狂划动。哪怕股市连续几个月完全漫无方向，我们总有东西可聊。

turns.en: I see a lot of people diving or tiptoeing, at least, into setting it up. It's honestly something... It seems like basically everything we've done and been moving towards has the potential to exacerbate single day volatility.
turns.zh: 我看到很多人一头扎进去、或至少小心翼翼地开始搭建它。老实说，这是我想要多研究很多的东西，因为我觉得它可能对市场结构有一些有意思的影响。比如，嘿，如果你有个 agent 在制定交易规则，那是不是意味着市面上的订单更少、止损更少？那会对市场可见度（market visibility）造成什么影响？诸如此类。所以我对这个、以及它会如何体现很感兴趣。而且我确实需要，我觉得，去跟更多「手指搭在按钮上」的人聊聊。但我真的认为它也有可能，再一次，加剧波动性。似乎基本上我们所做的、以及一直在朝之迈进的一切，都有可能加剧单日波动性。

Just the fact that this debt comes from kind of safe places. Right.
turns.zh: 对。广度不是我会拿来当作这件事的充分条件、甚至必要条件。我很无聊，我喜欢守住那个长期驱动股票的东西——它其实也在中期和短期帮着驱动股票——那就是盈利（earnings）。我最近研究了一下：如果你等到 S&P 500 的盈利修正离它的 52 周高点回落 5% 时再行动，会发生什么？如果你是这样的——我们都知道分析师是出了名的滞后，你肯定错过了顶部——但那会有多糟？你会差多远？在过去六七次熊市里，唯一一次你会因此被狠狠干掉的，就是新冠。只因为它发生得太快，根本没人有时间反应，等它发生时我们已经整个进入封锁了。但几乎其他每一次，即便在预估已经被下调之后你才入场、也就是明知自己迟到了，只要往后持有两年，大多数时候你仍能看到相当健康的收益。所以我的看法是：嘿，如果你一直持有仓位，你大概可以等得起，等到盈利开始在指数层面出现裂痕、给你某种要离场的预警信号。是的，除此之外，我觉得是像你们这样密切关注信用市场、以及那里正在发生的一些奇特现象的人，才最处在一个能看出「好吧，这种金融上的花活儿什么时候走过了头」的位置。因为我高度确信的一件事是：当 hyperscaler 的自由现金流（FCF）转负时，好，你现在有两个选择——要么 AI 繁荣放缓，要么融资开始变得更有「创意」。融资确实变得更有创意了。所以到某个点，这就值得琢磨，因为当你想眼下利润的来源：hyperscaler 的 CapEx，显然，而且其中更多是靠债务融资。而我们确实有一个很大的财政…… 赤字。那你能想出比 hyperscaler 债务和财政债务更安全的利润来源吗？那玩意儿相当安全——直到它不再安全为止，这就是你经典的那种 Minsky 式套路。所以老实说，有一点让我意外：估值倍数甚至没得到更多支撑，仅仅因为这些债务来自相当安全的地方。对。

But he points out it's like wars are very expensive. And he's like, is this like this is a third driver of inflationary impulse that doesn't get much attention. But defense spending rising for years all around the world.
turns.zh: 把话题拉回市场一小会儿。我收件箱里有一封有意思的报告，来自 Macquarie 的 Terry Wiseman。他指出，好吧，我们谈论这些巨大的支出冲劲等等，两个大头显然是 AI，然后是结构性的政府福利支出等，那个一直在往上。但他接着指出，战争真的非常烧钱。而市场上的人看待战争相关的头条，似乎主要是透过油价的镜头，对吧？以至于人们对 Iran 战争的交易兴趣基本上就是：好，这个什么时候能交易？什么时候开盘？油价是多少？也许是柴油价差。但他指出，战争非常昂贵。他说，这是不是第三个不太受关注的通胀冲劲驱动力？毕竟全球各地的国防开支已经连续多年上升。

turns.en: Yeah, wars are expensive, rearmaments expensive, trying to reshore and build domestic capacity of semiconductors is expensive. Yeah, all of this is really, really expensive. It is the defining feature of this era, like how much we are willing to kind of tolerate the side effects that are in our face every day of policies that are definitely bottom line inflationary.
turns.zh: 对，战争烧钱，重新武装（rearmament）烧钱，试图把半导体产能回流、在本土建起来也烧钱。是的，所有这些都非常、非常烧钱。这正是这个时代的一个定义性特征：我们愿意在多大程度上容忍那些每天摆在我们面前的副作用，而这些政策归根结底是通胀性的。

turns.en: Anything else really stand out for you right now as being kind of eye-opening in this market?
turns.zh: 眼下在这个市场里，还有没有别的什么让你觉得特别大开眼界的？

turns.en: I don't have much else. The only thing, I do think it is just borderline psycho that the idea that European equal weight is closer to an all-time high than U.S. equal weight when we're running around 6% nominal growth right now in the U.S. absolutely boggles my mind that U.S. consumer discretionary has become the new punching bag for the market in a strong growth environment. In a quarter where it's estimated to contribute, what, 2.8 percentage points to growth. Nuts, amazing.
turns.zh: 我没太多别的了。唯一一点：我确实觉得，European 等权指数比 U.S. 等权指数更接近历史高点，这简直近乎神经病——而此刻我们在 U.S. 的名义增长正跑在大约 6%。绝对让我难以置信：在强劲增长的环境下，U.S. 非必需消费（consumer discretionary）竟然成了市场新的「出气筒」。而在这个季度，它估计要贡献——多少来着——2.8 个百分点的增长。疯了，太神奇了。

turns.en: I guess one question I have in addition to that is, in a different era, there would have just been so much more attention to how bad the housing market is. It used to be housing was the business cycle. Well, A, housing was the business cycle for multiple reasons. People spent out of their home, equity, et cetera. Now we have this miserable punk housing market, and it hardly seems to matter.
turns.zh: 我想除了那个之外，我还有一个问题：换作别的时代，大家会对房市有多糟投入多得多的关注。过去，房市就是经济周期本身。嗯，首先，房市之所以是经济周期，有多重原因——人们靠房屋净值（home equity）消费，等等。而现在我们有一个惨淡、疲软的房市，它却几乎无关紧要。

turns.en: But now AI is the business cycle, which worries.
turns.zh: 但现在 AI 才是经济周期，这让人担心——

turns.en: Me because you get the same dynamic. And this wealth effect of people spending out of their stock market gains. I'm just curious, your take on, I don't know, either way you look at it, whether it's like The salience of the stock market and the wealth effect, or just the general market's lack of interest in housing these days.
turns.zh: ——担心我，因为你会得到同样的动态，还有这种财富效应（wealth effect）：人们靠股市收益来消费。我只是好奇你的看法，不管你从哪个角度看——是股市的显眼度和财富效应，还是市场对房市如今普遍缺乏兴趣。

turns.en: Well, perfect timing, right? It wasn't an earlier this year when Americans share wealth from stocks versus from housing also crossed overs. Yeah, it is a, it does feel like a seminal moment in that front. And when you think about why housing was the business cycle, it's because you, you had these spillover effects to consumption via HELOCs or just via wealth effect. from that and also, you know, spillovers from housing markets doing better, you're buying more consumer durables. You can just take all of that and transfer it over to AI, right? Like you can just take, that's where the construction impulse comes from. That's where the wealth impulse comes from. And as we've talked about, it's rivaling or surpassing everything we've ever done in terms of the CapEx boom in size. So do I think it lasts forever?
turns.zh: 嗯，时机正好，对吧？不就在今年早些时候，美国人来自股票的财富份额与来自房产的财富份额发生了交叉。是的，这确实感觉像是那个方面的一个开创性时刻。而当你想为什么房市曾是经济周期，是因为你有这些向消费的溢出效应——通过 HELOC（房屋净值信用额度），或者仅仅是通过由此而来的财富效应；还有房市向好带来的溢出，你会买更多耐用消费品。你可以把这一切原样搬到 AI 上，对吧？你可以直接搬过去——建筑冲劲就是这么来的，财富冲劲就是这么来的。而且正如我们谈到的，就 CapEx 繁荣的规模而言，它足以媲美、甚至超过我们以往做过的一切。所以我觉得它会永远持续吗？

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不会。

turns.en: Do I think it's kind of more of an anomaly around now?
turns.zh: 我觉得眼下它更像是一个反常现象吗？

turns.en: Certainly.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: Because like at the end of the day, we're all either businesses trying to make a profit or consumers trying to buy something we like. All of this has to eventually be good for somebody downstream at the end of this or else there is no point to anything we're doing. So there is no point to the profit if there's no kind of consumer intent for it in the long run and a consumer income to buy it.
turns.zh: 因为归根结底，我们要么是试图盈利的企业，要么是试图买自己喜欢东西的消费者。所有这些最终都必须对链条下游、末端的某个人有好处，否则我们所做的一切都毫无意义。所以，如果长期看没有消费者的购买意愿、没有消费者的收入去买它，那这份利润也就毫无意义。

turns.en: Yeah, the circularity and the size is what starts to worry you, I think. And when you hear that people are using their stocks, their stock market gains to buy stuff, which is helping the economy along, along with the AI CapEx build out, and that's leading to stock gains and relative economic growth. And then it just becomes very perpetual motion machining.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得正是那种循环性（circularity）和规模开始让你担心。当你听到人们用他们的股票、用他们的股市收益去买东西，这在推动经济，连同 AI 的 CapEx 建设，而那又带来股票收益和相对的经济增长。然后它就变成了一台非常「永动机」式的机器。

turns.en: Something that you've talked about for a long time that I've started to think about is like this idea of like something big is going to happen soon, right? And that big could be, it's like, oh, maybe there was like a major catastrophe like caused by a bot or whatever, or sorry, an AI model, or there's something big could be like Utopia and everyone, real weight, real wealth goes up dramatically and things get a lot cheaper, et cetera. Or there's something big could be a major reshuffling of people's place in the labor market in some way. But I'm curious whether like, okay, some thing that everyone just sort of has out there is going to happen, whether that leads to like a dip in the savings rate, because it's like, well, like, This, you know, that's a real thing yet.
turns.zh: 有一件你谈论了很久、而我也开始思考的事，就是这种「某件大事很快会发生」的想法，对吧？而那件「大事」可能是，哦，也许是一场由某个 bot、或者抱歉，某个 AI 模型引发的重大灾难；或者那件大事可能是乌托邦，每个人的实际财富（real wealth）大幅上升，东西变得便宜很多，等等；或者那件大事可能是人们在劳动力市场中的地位以某种方式被大洗牌。但我好奇的是，好吧，如果大家都隐隐觉得有这么一件「在那儿」的事要发生，这会不会导致储蓄率下滑？因为就像，嗯，你知道，这已经是一件真实存在的事了吗？

turns.en: It's the exact opposite of the, like, right. If you fear nuclear war, then just buy stocks anyways, because if it's in the price, I think now, like you could reasonably argue the other side, like, Hey, if, If the world's doomed in 10 years, why am I saving it all? I find that fun and interesting.
turns.zh: 这正好是那个的反面，对吧。如果你怕核战争，那就干脆照样买股票，因为如果它已经被 price in 了……我觉得现在你可以合理地论证另一面：嘿，如果世界 10 年后就完蛋了，我为什么还要把一切都存起来？我觉得这个又好玩又有意思。

turns.en: Do you think that's a real thing yet?
turns.zh: 你觉得这已经是一件真实存在的事了吗？

turns.en: I don't think if you're someone with children, you could possibly countenance the, hey, I'm going to sacrifice future welfare for that. So I don't think it's something that could gain broad traction. But in terms of infecting people's minds, I think we're kind of definitely already there.
turns.zh: 我不认为——如果你是一个有孩子的人，你可能会容忍这种「嘿，我要为此牺牲未来的福祉」的想法。所以我不认为这是能获得广泛认同的东西。但就「侵蚀人们的思想」而言，我觉得我们肯定已经到了那一步。

turns.en: If AI kills us all by setting off a nuclear weapon, our portfolios will be on fire.
turns.zh: 如果 AI 引爆核武器把我们全杀了，我们的投资组合会「火」一把。

turns.en: And you'll feel stupid for not having gone out to eat.
turns.zh: 而你会为自己没出去大吃一顿而觉得自己很蠢。

turns.en: If AI doesn't kill us all, then our portfolios will also be on fire.
turns.zh: 如果 AI 没把我们全杀了，那我们的投资组合也会「火」一把。

turns.en: That's a good one.
turns.zh: 这句妙。

turns.en: Thank you. I've tweeted that before, so I'm recycling my own jokes.
turns.zh: 谢谢。我以前发过这条推，所以我是在回收自己的段子。

turns.en: That's fine.
turns.zh: 没关系。

turns.en: That's fine.
turns.zh: 没关系。

turns.en: Luke, that was a lot of fun. I love your framing. Great stuff. Appreciate you coming back on Outbox.
turns.zh: Luke，这太有意思了。我喜欢你的框架。很棒。感谢你再次上 Odd Lots。

turns.en: Always a pleasure. Keep it up, guys. I love following and reading what you guys do.
turns.zh: 一直是种荣幸。继续加油，伙计们。我喜欢关注和阅读你们做的东西。

turns.en: There's a lot of fun. We could talk to Luke for hours. And I do think, you know, I went into this episode, it's like, oh, there's a crazy market. I love the speed characterization that Luke gave. I think that's perfect.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。我们能跟 Luke 聊上几个小时。我确实觉得，你知道，我做这期节目时想的是「哦，市场真疯狂」。我很喜欢 Luke 给出的「速度」这个刻画。我觉得那太到位了。

turns.en: No, I think that makes a lot of sense. And again, in my mind, there's two things happening here, which is you have a change in the actual structure and makeup of the market. And you also have just the headlines flying thick and fast. It's so hard to keep up. And if you see one negative headline on a Monday, chances are you might see a positive headline on a Tuesday. Even if you don't believe the positive headlines, you know the markets will react to them. And so you're just sort of ping-ponging back and forth between the news flow.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得这很有道理。而且再说一次，在我脑子里，这里有两件事在同时发生：一是市场实际的结构和构成发生了变化；二是头条新闻铺天盖地、飞来飞去，太难跟上了。如果你周一看到一条负面头条，很可能周二就会看到一条正面头条。哪怕你不信那些正面头条，你也知道市场会对它们作出反应。所以你就在新闻流里来回乒乓。

turns.en: I want to build something like where we just look. The history of red headlines would be an interesting... chart right yeah and it would be really curious to look over trends about the pacing of them there's got to be some way to do.
turns.zh: 我想搭个什么东西，让我们就看——「红色头条」的历史会是一张有意思的……图，对吧，是的；而去看它们节奏上的趋势会非常让人好奇。总得有办法做到这一点。

turns.en: That one thing i'd be interested in it used to be the case with early machine reading trading as we used to call it no one calls it that anymore that people would actually step away when there was a big headline so there was a little bit of a dip in liquidity because it took like a second for a lot of the machines to read the news and like figure out how to react I doubt that's the case anymore. I would be very curious to see what liquidity provision actually looks like around headlines. But I don't know if anyone's done a study.
turns.zh: 有一件事我会很感兴趣：过去在早期的「机器读取交易」（machine reading trading）——我们以前这么叫，现在没人这么叫了——那时候一有重大头条，人们真的会退场，所以流动性会有一点下降，因为很多机器需要大约一秒钟去读新闻、琢磨怎么反应。我怀疑现在还是不是这样。我非常好奇想看到，在头条前后流动性提供实际上是什么样子。但我不知道有没有人做过研究。

turns.en: I worry about plenty of things.
turns.zh: 我担心的事可多了。

turns.en: Okay. Shall we leave it there?
turns.zh: 好吧。我们就聊到这儿？

turns.zh: 就聊到这儿吧。
